message.content:
**Hydrogen (H)** – the simplest and most abundant element in the universe – has a rich set of physical, chemical, and nuclear properties that make it unique among the elements. Below is a concise overview of its key characteristics:

| Property | Value / Description |
|----------|---------------------|
| **Atomic number** | 1 |
| **Symbol** | H |
| **Standard atomic weight** | ~1.008 u (average of isotopes) |
| **Electron configuration** | 1s¹ |
| **Isotopes** | Protium (^1H, 99.98 %), Deuterium (^2H, 0.02 %) – stable; Tritium (^3H) – radioactive (half‑life ≈12.32 yr). |
| **Melting point** | –259.16 °C (14 K) – solidifies as ice at very low temperatures. |
| **Boiling point** | –252.87 °C (20.28 K) – gaseous under normal conditions. |
| **Density** | 0.08988 g L⁻¹ at 25 °C (≈0.0000899 kg m⁻³). |
| **Molar volume** | 22.414 L mol⁻¹ at 0 °C, 1 atm (ideal gas). |
| **Color** | Colorless |
| **Odor** | Odorless |
| **Taste** | Tasteless |
| **State at STP** | Gas |
| **Electronegativity (Pauling)** | 2.20 |
| **First ionization energy** | 13.598 eV (1312 kJ mol⁻¹) |
| **Second ionization energy** | 24.587 eV (2375 kJ mol⁻¹) |
| **Electron affinity** | –72.8 kJ mol⁻¹ (negative, meaning energy is released when an electron is added). |
| **Heat capacity (Cp)** | 28.836 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ at 298 K |
| **Thermal conductivity** | 0.180 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ at 300 K |
| **Electrical conductivity** | Very low in neutral form; becomes high when ionized (plasma). |
| **Reactivity** | Highly reactive with many metals (forming hydrides), oxidizes readily in air (combustion → water vapor). |
| **Flammability** | Extremely flammable; forms explosive mixtures with air (range 4–75 % by volume). |
| **Combustion reaction** | 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O (exothermic, ΔH° ≈ –286 kJ mol⁻¹). |
| **Bonding** | Forms covalent bonds (H–H single bond), ionic bonds (as H⁺ or H⁻ in acids/base chemistry). |
| **Acidity/Basicity** | Acts as a weak acid (hydronium formation) and a weak base (hydride formation). |
| **Spectral lines** | Lyman series (UV), Balmer series (visible), Paschen series (IR) – fundamental in astrophysics. |
| **Applications** | Fuel (gasoline, fuel cells), rocket propellant (liquid hydrogen), industrial feedstock (ammonia synthesis, methanol production), cryogenic cooling, medical imaging (MRI contrast agents using deuterated compounds). |

### Key Highlights

- **Lightest Element**: With only one proton and one electron, hydrogen is the lightest element, giving it the lowest density and highest specific energy content per unit mass.
- **Isotopic Variants**: Deuterium and tritium are used in nuclear fusion research and in labeling studies in chemistry and biology.
- **Chemical Behavior**: Hydrogen’s ability to form both covalent and ionic bonds makes it central to organic chemistry, biochemistry, and materials science.
- **Physical Extremes**: It remains gaseous down to extremely low temperatures, and its boiling point is close to absolute zero, making it useful for cryogenic applications.
- **Energy Carrier**: In fuel cells, hydrogen reacts with oxygen to produce electricity, heat, and water—an attractive clean‑energy pathway.

These properties collectively explain why hydrogen is so important across scientific disciplines—from astrophysics (spectral lines reveal stellar composition) to renewable energy technologies (fuel cells, hydrogen storage).
